# The Unfamiliar Country

Five years. Five years in the same place, walking the same streets, greeting the same faces—and yet nothing here belongs to me, and I belong to none of it. The people I pass wear expressions I should recognize, speak in voices that should be worn smooth by familiarity, and still they arrive as strangers each morning, as though the world resets itself while I sleep and forgets to include me in its reconstruction. There is a particular loneliness in this, in being unrecognized by the recognizable, in standing at the center of one's own life and feeling like an intruder.

The white returns to me again and again. White wolves moving at the edge of thought, their coats too bright, too clean for the dim places they inhabit. And beneath the blistering paint of these old walls, where the surface swells and cracks and finally gives way, there is that same white—the raw substrate exposed, the thing that was always underneath, revealed at last against its will. I cannot say what the whiteness means, only that it unsettles me, that it seems to promise a truth I am not prepared to see. Some things are painted over for a reason.

Then comes the doctor, always the doctor, intruding upon the private disorder of my mind with his clinical patience. He makes me repeat the words back to him. *Chimera*, he says, and waits. *Chimera*, I answer, and the word tastes strange in my mouth, a creature stitched together from mismatched parts, a diagnosis dressed as mythology. What is he testing? What is he trying to draw out of me, or perhaps to put in? The white room, the steady voice, the words handed back and forth between us like specimens under glass.

I have begun to catalog what I fear. (The fear of dreaming, of what waits behind closed eyes.) (The fear of bearing a monster, of carrying something inside me that should never be born.) (The fear of not being at home, even here, even now, even in this place I have inhabited for five long years.) The parentheses contain them, but they cannot contain them; the fears leak out around the edges of every ordinary hour.

And everywhere, the decay. The window frames have rotted in their sockets, the putty crumbling away in dry gray flakes that gather on the sill. The Victorian buildings shed their skins along the whole length of the street, paint curling back from brick, ornament softening into ruin. It is as though the outer world has agreed to mirror the inner one—to peel and rot and give way in exact sympathy with whatever is peeling and rotting in me. Perhaps this is why nothing feels familiar. Perhaps I have simply watched too long as everything, including myself, comes slowly apart.
outputs.L4:
**The Familiar Made Strange**

There are wolves in the trees again. I count them the way I count the cracks that run like rivers across the ceiling—one, two, a third that hides itself behind the light fixture. They do not move. Wolves in trees do not move. This is how I know they are watching. *(dendrophobia: the fear of trees, or perhaps only the fear of what waits inside them.)*

The window frame is rotting. I press my thumb against the wood and it gives like fruit, soft and yielding, weeping a dark moisture I do not want to name. When did the house begin to decay? When did the walls forget their function? I lived here once. I am almost certain I lived here once. *(oikophobia: the fear of home, of the rooms that once held you.)*

Somewhere below, a door I have never opened. A hallway that leads to a hallway. The floorboards remember footsteps that are not mine and repeat them softly in the dark. *(agoraphobia, no—the opposite—the fear of the small room closing, the fear of the known becoming unknowable.)*

I look at my hands and they are a stranger's hands. Pale, unfamiliar, the fingers too long, the knuckles wrong. I flex them and feel the movement arrive a half-second late, as though I am commanding a body from very far away, through water, through years. Is this my body? Was it ever? *(depersonalization: the sensation that you are watching yourself from just behind your own shoulder.)*

The wolves have multiplied. Now there are five, now seven, their eyes the color of the streetlight that has never worked. The trees hold them like offerings. The trees have always held them. I only forgot to look. *(nyctophobia: the fear of the dark, of what the dark permits.)*

Everything in this room insists that it belongs here—the chair, the lamp, the photograph of people I should recognize. Their smiles are correct. Their faces are correct. And yet a cold certainty rises in me: I have never seen them before. The room is a stage set for a life I was supposed to live and did not. *(jamais vu: the terror of the familiar arriving as if for the first time.)*

The window weeps. The wolves wait. My hands are not my hands. And still the walls contract, breathing in, breathing in, never out—

*(basophobia: the fear of falling, though I have not moved.)*

I stay very still. I have learned that stillness is the only prayer the house accepts. Outside, or perhaps inside, or perhaps in the narrow country between the two, the trees lean closer to the glass. Something in me recognizes this as the moment before. Before what, I cannot say.

The clock does not tick. It has never ticked. I only imagined the sound to fill the silence where my heartbeat should be. *(thanatophobia: the fear of death, or the stranger fear that death has already happened and no one thought to tell you.)*

There are wolves in the trees again.

There have always been wolves in the trees.

I am the one who keeps forgetting.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an experimental prose poem that weaves together fragments of gothic horror, phobia definitions in parentheses, and a fractured domestic scene, numbered in sections.
counterfactuals.output:
# Inheritance, or The House That Names Its Rooms

**1.**

Mother sets the table for six though we are three. (*Arithmophobia: the fear of numbers, of what they insist upon.*) The forks lie down like small silver bodies. Outside, the wisteria has learned to knock.

**2.**

There is a door in the hallway that was not there when the deed was signed. I have counted the doors. I have counted them again. The house disagrees with my counting. (*Oikophobia: the fear of one's home, of the familiar turned strange in the hand.*)

**3.**

Father's coat still hangs by the entrance, though Father—
though Father is a subject we do not
the coat still holds the shape of shoulders
we do not

**4.**

(*Aphephobia: the fear of being touched.*) My sister will not let the banister hold her. She descends each stair as though the wood remembers something her body has agreed to forget. The portraits watch this. The portraits have always watched this.

**5.**

In the kitchen: the smell of bread that no one baked. Mother says *eat*. Mother says *we are so happy here*. Mother's smile is a drawer that will not close. (*Phagophobia: the fear of swallowing, of taking the house inside you.*)

**6.**

The cellar breathes in winter. I have pressed my ear to the floor and heard the foundations reciting our names in an older order, an order that precedes us, that will outlast the roof, the deed, the small silver bodies of the forks.

**7.**

(*Athazagophobia: the fear of being forgotten. The fear of forgetting.*)

**8.**

My sister asks: *Do you remember the garden?* And I say yes though I remember nothing, though the word *garden* opens in me like a room I have never entered, wallpapered in a green that was never a color, only a suggestion the eyes agreed to.

**9.**

Mother sets the table for six. The two empty chairs are not empty. This is the first thing the house teaches. The second thing the house teaches is that *empty* was always the wrong word. (*Kenophobia: the fear of voids, of vacant spaces, of the pause before the answer.*)

**10.**

At night the wisteria knocks and knocks and I go to no door, I open no door, I count the doors instead—one, two, a number that will not hold still, a number that grows a face—and somewhere beneath the floor the foundations say my name

in the old order

in the order that means *stay*

*stay*

*stay.*
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.output:
# The House That Wore My Face

*a collage*

---

"The better to see you with," said the window,
though I'd never trusted glass to tell the truth.

—

**FIVE YEARS.** The doormat says WELCOME
in a font I don't remember choosing.

—

Grandmother, what large panes you have.
What long shadows across the kitchen floor,
where I once—did I ever?—drank my coffee
facing east, or was it always
the other wall, the one now painted
a color called *Reclaimed.*

—

> *"The wolf came to the window and looked in,
> and the little ones knew him by his voice."*

But this is the trouble:
I know this house by its voice
and cannot place the accent.

—

Three little rooms.
Not by the hair on my chinny-chin-chin
did I recognize the third,
where the light falls wrong,
where someone hung a mirror
at the height of a stranger.

—

**INVENTORY OF THE UNCANNY:**
- the stair that used to creak (silent now, or lying)
- a key that fits, a lock that hesitates
- my mother's handwriting on a box marked FRAGILE / KITCHEN
- the smell of a childhood
   that belongs to a different child

—

*What big windows,*
all the better to be seen through—
to stand inside your own front room
and feel the wolf-lope of your pulse,
the fairy-tale certainty
that something has been swapped,
some changeling architecture,
some house wearing my house
like a wolf in grandmother's nightgown.

—

> "Open the window," said the girl,
> "so I can hear the forest breathing."

I open every window.
The forest has moved closer.
Or the house has walked, somnambulant,
five years into a wood
I don't remember planting.

—

Home is the place where,
when you go there,
they have to change the locks,
repaint the walls,
grow a stranger in the glass
who waves back
a half-second too late.

—

Little pig, little pig,
let me in.

*But I am already inside,
and I have forgotten
which one of us
is knocking.*
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.output:
# The House That Was Ours

The wallpaper (they call this *automatonophobia*, the dread of things that should be still but seem to move) peels in strips like skin from a fruit gone soft, and I remember when the pattern meant something—roses, or perhaps

perhaps they were always faces.

Mother's chair. Mother's chair sits where it always sat. But the angle. The *angle* is wrong now (there is no proper word for this, the terror of furniture rearranged by no hand), tilted three degrees toward the door as if it had been listening, as if it had turned to watch me enter and thought better of it.

---

The banister remembers my palm. That is the trouble. It *remembers* me sliding down its curve as a child and now the wood has grown warm in the shape of a hand that is not my hand, smaller, the fingers

(where did the fingers go)

The stairs count wrong going up. Thirteen. Always thirteen. But last night—fourteen, and the fourteenth exhaled beneath my weight like something breathing that had been holding its breath since 1887.

---

*Here is the kitchen where she made the bread.*
*Here is the kitchen.*
*Here is the*

The smell is right. That's what undoes me. The rot smells like rising dough (*there should be a phobia for this, the fear that comfort and decay share a scent*) and the ceiling sags with old water like a lung filling, and I know—I KNOW—that if I open the pantry the jars will be full and gleaming, preserved, the peaches suspended in their syrup like specimens, like eyes,

watching from behind glass the way the whole house watches, patient, familiar, wearing the face of home the way a body wears

a face

---

I have lived here always.
I have never seen this place before.

Both are true and this is the disease of it (call it *lachanophobia* if the rooms have started growing something in the corners, pale and reaching), the way the known becomes the *almost*-known, the uncanny threshold where my own reflection in the hallway mirror

pauses

a half-second too long before it agrees to be me.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

# Ledger of the Unwaking

**1.**
Woke before the alarm again. The ceiling
had the wrong number of corners.
I counted four but felt a fifth
breathing in the arithmetic.

**2.**
Note to self: the coffee tasted like
a rehearsal. Everything lately is a rehearsal for
—

**4.**
(skipped 3. 3 is where the dread lives.
I leave it empty like a chair
pulled out for someone who is late
by years.)

**5.**
Dreamt the city was made of my own teeth.
Walked its molars. The rent was memory.
I paid in faces I no longer

**5. (again)**
—recognize. The doctor says déjà vu
is just the brain filing a moment
in the wrong drawer. So why does the drawer
keep opening on its own—

**7.**
Skipped 6 too. Getting easier
to skip. Getting easier to be a gap
where a person used to sit.
Today my hands felt borrowed.
I gave them back nothing.

**8.**
Rained. Or the window performed rain.
Hard to tell the difference
between weather and its rumor.
I pressed my palm to the glass and the glass
pressed back, colder than agreement.

**11.**
The numbers are leaving without me now.
This is fine. This is—

**?**
Woke inside the dream I had last Tuesday,
the one I thought I'd finished.
Turns out dreams don't end.
They only lose your address.

**12.**
Reminder: buy bread. Water the—
who am I speaking to.
The diary assumes a reader.
The reader assumes a life.
Both of us are guessing.

**13.**
I looked in the mirror and it took
a full second to load.
In that second: no one.
In that second: the truest photograph
of me ever taken.

**14. (the last one, probably)**
If I stop numbering
does the day stop counting.
If I close the book
does the dread go home
or does it move in, unpack,
hang its coat on the fifth corner
I always knew was

**Say It Again**

say *house* the doctor says and I say *house*
but the word has gone soft in my mouth like wet plaster
say it again he says *again again*
and behind him the window frame is weeping
brown-black rot blooming from the corners
the wood remembering it was once a tree
was once alive was once *say it* he says *tree*

and I am four years old with the fat blue crayon
drawing the wolf my mother pinned above the sink
white as an unwritten page white as a swallowed pill
four crooked legs and one enormous eye
looking looking always looking at the drawer
where the knives sleep

*wolf* he says and I say *wolf*
but a wolf came to the window last winter didn't it
pressed its long clean skull against the rotten sill
and the frame gave way like something forgiven
and it did not enter it only breathed
white breath white fur white white
*repeat after me* and I forget the word

the doctor's face is a drawing too
somebody's hurried hand a smudge for a mouth
say *safe* he says and I try but *safe* dissolves
the way a name dissolves when you say it forty times
until it is only sound only weather only
*again*

there were wolves in the wallpaper of my childhood
I traced them with a crayon they never asked me to
crude and holy their teeth were little houses
and every house had a window
and every window had begun to rot
from the inside from the swelling breath
of something white and patient in the yard

*look at me* he says *say your name*
and I open my mouth and out comes fur
and out comes the smell of wet wood breaking
and out comes a drawing of a door I never
opened
*again* he says
*again*

but the window is open now
and the wolves are so quiet
and I have forgotten every word
except the one he keeps
making me
say
